1p3c0x1:181: The paper's conclusions cannot be extrapolated unconditionally. The study is explicitly limited to the "high compute, data-scarce" regime—an extreme scenario where compute is abundant but available data (especially high-quality data) is relatively insufficient; in this case, keeping all data provides more learning signals to the model. For the common pretraining scenario with abundant data and limited compute, filtering remains a necessary means to control training cost and improve sample efficiency. Understanding the experimental setup is a prerequisite for correctly applying the conclusions: directly transplanting "don't filter" into a data-rich pipeline may backfire.
1sbow0v:198: Through scaling studies specifically targeting the high-compute, data-scarce regime, the paper finds that as training compute and model size grow, the benefits of data filtering gradually disappear or even turn negative. The authors' proposed explanation is that, after sufficient training, large models can extract signals from "noise" on their own; data that is nominally low-quality or treated as distractors actually provides broader distribution coverage and additional regularization signals, helping the model learn more robust representations.
1sf0dqj:306: This paper (arXiv:2605.19407, by Christopher Mohri, John Duchi, and Tatsunori Hashimoto) investigates data filtering in large-model pretraining through new scaling studies aimed at the "high compute, data-scarce" regime. The core finding is counterintuitive and striking: when compute is sufficient, the best data filter is no filter—adequately trained large-parameter models not only tolerate low-quality and distractor data, but actually benefit from it. This conclusion directly challenges the mainstream belief that pretraining must filter for high-quality data, and resonates deeply with Rich Sutton's "Bitter Lesson."

cfyweg:221: Any filtering pipeline implicitly embeds a set of assumptions about "what is worth learning": quality scorers, heuristic rules, and deduplication thresholds are essentially ways of writing human inductive biases into the training pipeline. The hidden costs include: building and maintaining filtering criteria requires significant human effort; quality criteria (e.g., perplexity, rule scores) are often misaligned with downstream task objectives; and more critically, filtering can systematically discard long-tail information useful for generalization. The paper's findings suggest that, given sufficient scale, letting models face unfiltered data and extract signals on their own may outperform human-designed filtering.

vydtwj:214: Rich Sutton's classic lesson is that decades of AI research show that building human knowledge directly into systems often wins early but loses late, while the path of general methods (search, learning) plus scaled compute ultimately prevails. This paper extends that logic to data engineering: filtering rules are one form of "injecting human intuitive judgments about data quality into the learning process." The experimental results show that when compute is large enough, such human priors are not only unnecessary but may even harm the model's ability to learn from the original data distribution—another confirmation of the Bitter Lesson on the data dimension.
